posts.title: Show HN: I spent 2 years designing a mechanical Magic Keyboard
posts.author: aemerson_
posts.post_text:
Hi HN, today I’m revealing Altar II, an ultra-low profile (4.75mm) mechanical keyboard designed to replace your Magic Keyboard. It’s the keyboard I wish Apple made.

Altar II has fully mechanical switches, plus a magnetically detachable dial, haptic feedback, a red backlight, and a native macOS companion app.

I’m a heavy Mac user and I feel that Apple hasn’t given its keyboards the attention they deserve, in terms of hardware, software, and features, so I set out to try and change that.

It was a massive undertaking and it has taken almost 2 years to get to this stage. One of the main obstacles was fitting a reasonably sized battery into the chassis, and aggressive power profiling without messing with the user experience. Another issue was we couldn’t fit any components on the underside of the PCB because there was literally no space to do so (and there are a lot of components).

Around 4 years ago I posted my first keyboard to HN (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=32507172). Its response blew me away and ultimately led to me quitting my job and making and selling keyboards full time. I’ve taken some of the feedback from that original post and incorporated it into Altar II (e.g. the detachable dial).

I’ll be around to answer any questions. Please let me know what you think, I’d love to get some feedback.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tB3lk-PNA6I
As near as I can understand it, macOS supports a smart card reader (and apparently will defer to its sign-off for authentication duties when it's present and configured, and Touch ID isn't), so if you emulate a smart card reader you can make your own fingerprint sensor and have it say "I'm a smart card" and sign challenges like a smart card does.
The creator is very up front that this isn't equivalently secure for preserving state secrets, as if you carefully tear this device apart you can just short the pins that the sensor part connects when it's happy with the fingerprint. On the other hand, it is hilarious that anyone who isn't a person of interest for the CIA, Mossad, MI6, or FSB would think they're important enough for someone to go to the trouble of using that method to unlock their secrets. Anyone else would just club you over the head or slip you a mickey, and stick your unconscious finger on your fingerprint sensor.

replies.text:
The usual way of doing backlight is by having the LED underneath the switch and letting the switch transmit the light upwards. Many switches have special cutout positions for this, so the lighting for all the square keys is identical.
The only issue is that the keycap itself needs to be partially translucent and partially opaque, so rather than laser-etching or printing a legend they need to be "double-shot"[0], which means a two-phase injection molding process. This makes altering of the keycaps quite expensive as you need a new set of molds - which is 
especially
 bad if you were using one mold to produce an entire set of keycaps at once.
It's definitely 
doable
 to ship it with two different number rows, but it's the kind of thing you really want to know at the very start.
[0]: 
https://deskthority.net/wiki/Double-shot_moulding

posts.title: Ask HN: Did GitHub remove the stargazers list?
posts.author: reconnecting
posts.post_text:
GitHub seems to be continuing (1) to deprecate star information. First the stargazers list was hidden from logged-out users, and now the main stargazers link on repo pages has disappeared too. /stargazers returns a 404 (2) unless you own the repo.

I know many people say stars aren't a real signal, but they were: they made it possible to detect signs of bought stars. Some third-party services even showed the geographic distribution of a repo's stars so you could judge whether they looked fake.

The main point is that whatever reasoning GitHub offers, the outcome is the same: either GitHub is weak against bots, or it would rather control these signals itself, with no way for outsiders to audit them.

1. https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48821803

2. https://github.com/tirrenotechnologies/tirreno/stargazers

posts.title: Ask HN: Anyone interested in building a harness-only benchmark?
posts.author: GodelNumbering
posts.post_text:
There are a lot of LLM benchmarks but few, if any, harness benchmarks. I am thinking this would be a really good community project to build one.

End goal: a leaderboard of harness performance (multiple axis) on a set of diverse real world tasks[1], grouped by underlying models and reasoning efforts. Anyone can contribute results.

The task criteria, measurements, underlying framework et al can be decided by a group rather than a single person.

If there is sufficient interest, I will create a discord.

Disclosure: I am the maintainer of a coding agent called Dirac (https://github.com/dirac-run/dirac) so I will not influence what the final benchmark should look like to avoid any conflict of interest. I just want to make this happen.

[1] Diverse real world tasks meaning sufficiently complex tasks that the contributors have encountered, preferably from an opensource repo.

posts.title: Ask HN: What would make you list your AI product on a new marketplace?
posts.author: Achrima
posts.post_text:
Right now the AI tool that wins is the one with the biggest marketing budget and hype, not the one that works best.

We want a marketplace where sellers have to show proof, so buyers can tell the difference before they pay. We are trying to bring proof and quality to the AI market.

We are building it now. It is not open yet, and before we go further we want to know what would actually make someone list on it.

If you sell an AI tool: what has gone wrong for you on existing marketplaces and directories? What would make you list on a new one, and what would make you walk away?

While building it we made two free tools, no signup.

The Achboard reads any AI product's website like a sceptical buyer would.

Comparima shows a product next to its closest alternatives with what each costs.

Both at achrima.com

posts.title: Ask HN: Why mobile software infrastructure never belongs to its owner?
posts.author: rezvovmobile
posts.post_text:
There’s one question that’s been on my mind lately.

Over the past twenty years, we’ve learnt to take ownership of virtually any digital infrastructure.

But why does mobile software infrastructure still almost never belong to its owner? Is there a fundamental technical reason for this, or is it more a matter of economics, ecosystems and market habits?

I’d be particularly interested to hear the views of engineers who have worked on the architecture of mobile platforms or major mobile products for iOS and Android.

Perhaps I’m simply overlooking some fundamental limitation.
